current_episode.title: #46 He Had $12,000 and a Lucky Pineapple. Now Royalty Wears His Shoes | Edgardo Osorio, Founder & Creative Director of Aquazzura

guest.bio_context: Edgardo started working in the fashion industry at age 15 as an intern for a Colombian designer, then studied accessories in London and worked as a consultant for Ferragamo starting at age 19. By age 25, he had spent nearly 10 years in the industry before founding Aquazzura in 2012. He relocated to Florence to work directly with Italian artisans and manufacturers, establishing himself in Palazzo Corzini.

context.transcript_excerpt: If you're not comfortable, you can't be sexy. That's the hardest thing. I got into shoes by pure chance. And I was living in my factory. By the time I was 25, I'd been in the industry for almost 10 years. It's now to every generation. I love, love, love when I see a mother coming with her daughter, coming with her grandmother, and they all get to shop. I love that. And in the end, if you have a good product, you don't need the best marketing in the world. The product should sell itself. The luxury industry is full of brands that belong to conglomerates. Houses that were founded by individuals and now are run by committees. creative directors who cycle through every two years leaving no trace of themselves behind and in the middle of all of that there's a handful of founders who have chosen to stay independent to have their own vision and to build slowly with time and some of them that even thought to put a golden pineapple on the sole of every shoe as a lucky charm because they believe in positive energy and bringing that radiance from the bottom up. This is a conversation about what it means to build a luxury brand on your own terms, about those tensions between the creative freedom and the commercial pressure, about how founder-led models might be the most valuable asset in luxury right now, and about the anatomy of desire, how to make someone fall in love with a product that you do not need, but you cannot stop thinking about. Because as Gabrielle Chanel said, luxury is the necessity that begins when necessity ends. I'm Carla Torodbend, your host and founder of Beyond Luxury, a strategic advisory and media platform guiding top leaders in brands on the future of luxury and beyond. My guest today is one of the last true independent entrepreneurs in the industry. Edgardo Osorio is the founder and creative director of Acquazura, a brand that has become instantly iconic since its debut in 2012. Handmade in Italy with a focus in comfort and wearability, his creations combine luxury and craftsmanship with innovation, design and vibrant colors that give beautiful palettes. He lived between Colombia, Miami, London, before choosing to establish himself in Florence, inside the spectacular setting of Palazzo Corzini, in the heart of the Italian art and capital of the best shoemakers and artisans in the world. In just over a decade, Acquazura has transformed into a true lifestyle brand. The Casa Collection launched in 2022 with four tableware lines inspired by the passion of interior design and art de la table. A handbag line followed in 2023. And in 2025, a sunglass collection reimagining eyewear as objects of art. His shoes have been worn by Hollywood, from Cate Blanchett and Nicole Kidman to Beyonce and Rihanna, by fashion icons like Kate Moss and Naomi Campbell, and by royalty including the Princess of Wales, Queen Rania of Jordan, and Queen Maxima of the Netherlands. Aguazura is now available at over 300 retailers in 58 countries with flagship boutiques in Florence, New York, Doha, Jakarta, and many more. The pineapple on every soul is not a logo, it's a philosophy, a symbol of wealth, of prosperity, and hospitality that Edgardo collected long before the brand ever existed. We are talking about independence in the air of consolidation, the psychology of a lucky charm, and what happens when you build a lifestyle brand from the soul up. pending_qa.q: What is the symbolic meaning and placement strategy behind a luxury shoe brand's signature design element?
pending_qa.r: The gold pineapple on the sole of every Aquazzura shoe serves as a lucky charm and symbol of wealth, prosperity, and hospitality. Edgardo placed it on the bottom of the foot deliberately, referencing reflexology and the belief that energy flows through the feet, so wearing a lucky charm daily on the sole brings positive energy from the bottom up. He chose the pineapple because he had been collecting them since childhood and appreciated that it functions as a symbol rather than a traditional logo.

pending_qa.q: Why did relocating to Florence prove essential for a shoe designer's ability to execute complex handmade designs?
pending_qa.r: Edgardo chose to live in Florence and work directly in factories because Italy is a country of small, family-run manufacturers with deep expertise. Being physically present allowed him to build human relationships with artisans, pattern makers, and technicians who needed to understand his taste and vision. He explained that sending designs by email from London or New York is not the same—you need to work in the room with them, discover archival techniques, and build trust over time, which typically takes one and a half to two years for new technicians to master his signature style.

pending_qa.q: How did early financial constraints shape a founder's hands-on approach to quality control and brand building?
pending_qa.r: When Edgardo launched Aquazzura with just $12,000 in his bank account, he had no budget for a technical team or quality control department, so he personally opened every single box, checked every shoe, and touched each one before it was sold. He viewed this as an opportunity to bless each pair with the pineapple's luck and ensure every customer would be happy and feel great. This direct engagement became foundational to the brand's philosophy, even as it grew.

pending_qa.q: What role does a product's intrinsic quality play in a luxury brand's growth without heavy marketing investment?
pending_qa.r: Edgardo emphasized that if you have a good product, you don't need the best marketing in the world—the product should sell itself. When he started, he had no marketing money and relied entirely on word of mouth, with women wearing his shoes and recommending them to friends, mothers, and sisters. He stated that while beautiful marketing and stores are helpful extras, the brand starts and ends with the product, and the product needs to be good and thoughtfully designed for who will wear it, for what, and why.

pending_qa.q: How does designing for wearability rather than magazine photography change a shoe's structural and aesthetic outcome?
pending_qa.r: Edgardo contrasts two design philosophies: designing an object to be photographed beautifully versus designing for someone to wear it and feel better in it. When designers create beautiful objects for shelves or magazines without considering the person wearing them, the shoe doesn't work on the foot—it cuts the leg, looks uncomfortable, or makes the foot look square. He designs by cutting the shoe around the model throughout the process, ensuring the foot looks long, the toe cleavage is perfect, and every millimeter is proportional, because a millimeter or two in a shoe can make it uncomfortable or look off.

pending_qa.q: How did a multicultural background spanning Colombia, Miami, London, and Europe influence a luxury brand's global appeal?
pending_qa.r: Edgardo's diverse background—growing up in Colombia, spending four to five months yearly in Miami during childhood, studying in London, and eventually settling in Europe—gave him exposure to multiple markets and sensibilities. He travels nine months per year by choice and has friends across India, South America, Europe, Thailand, and the United States. This multicultural perspective allows his designs to resonate across different cultures: Brazilian women, Russian women, and Saudi women can all connect with and love his brand, making it accessible to customers from 18 to 70 years old across all generations.
